blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 4 (Molecular Biology (chapter banner printed as 'Biomolecules')), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Organic molecules make up most of the dry mass of protoplasm. (i) What are organic molecules and functional groups? (ii) Explain macromolecules and polymers, giving the percentage of the major organic molecules in dry mass. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Organic molecules are molecules synthesized by cells and containing carbon; they occur naturally only in living bodies or their products and remains. They have a carbon-based core to which special groups of atoms, functional groups (OH, CO, COOH, NH₂), are attached. Most biochemical reactions transfer a functional group from one molecule to another or break a carbon-carbon bond.

(ii) Most organic molecules are large and are called macromolecules. Many are polymers: molecules of many identical units called monomers. Carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids are polymers of sugars, amino acids and nucleotides respectively.
Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids make 93% of dry mass (Table 4.1): proteins 50%, nucleic acids 18%, carbohydrates 15%, lipids 10%. The remaining 7% is small organic molecules (vitamins) and inorganic molecules (CO₂, acids, bases, salts).

book_ref.quote: Most of the organic molecules are large in size and biologists call them macromolecules

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the types of bonds and interactions found in biological molecules and give the role of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Covalent bond: formed when two atoms share electrons. Often found in organic molecules like proteins and nucleic acids, giving them stability.
2. Ionic bond: one atom donates an electron (becomes a cation) and another accepts it (becomes an anion); the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is the bond. Relatively strong in the solid state; formed mostly in inorganic molecules like sodium chloride.
3. Hydrogen bond: weak attraction between a hydrogen atom and an electronegative atom (oxygen or nitrogen). Maintains the structure of proteins and nucleic acids and is important in processes like DNA replication.
4. Hydrophobic interactions: nonpolar molecules cluster together in water to minimize contact with water. Crucial for folding of proteins and formation of lipid bilayers in membranes.
5. Hydrophilic interactions: between polar molecules and water. Essential for dissolving polar and ionic compounds; help nutrient transport and chemical reactions in cells.
Carbon itself is tetravalent: its C-H bond is the source of chemical energy, its C-O glycosidic linkages stabilize carbohydrates and its C-N peptide bonds form proteins.

book_ref.quote: Different types of bonds and interactions play vital roles in the structure and function of biological molecules

blocks.prompt: 3 Define hydrolysis. Explain how it is the reverse of condensation, using the example of maltose, and give its importance. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hydrolysis: a chemical process in which a macromolecule (polymer) is broken down into smaller fragments by the addition of water molecules.

Condensation (dehydration synthesis): monomers join to make a polymer; an -OH group is removed from one monomer and an -H atom from another, i.e. a water molecule is removed. Energy is needed, so cells must supply energy to make macromolecules. Example: two glucose monomers join to form maltose.

Hydrolysis is the reverse: cells break the bond between monomers by adding water. The OH group of the water molecule joins one monomer and the hydrogen joins the second monomer. Example: maltose + water gives two glucose monomers.

Importance: breakdown of macromolecules is essential in digestion and cellular respiration, where smaller molecules are needed for energy production; H⁺ and OH⁻ ions of water take part in it.

book_ref.quote: Cells break bonds between monomers by adding water to them

blocks.prompt: 4 Explain the solvent property of water. How do sodium chloride and glucose dissolve in it? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Water dissolves a wide variety of substances due to two properties: the polarity of its molecules and their ability to form hydrogen bonds.

Polarity: the water molecule has distinct ends with partial charges; hydrogen is partially positive and oxygen partially negative. The partial negative end of one molecule attracts the partial positive end of another; this weak attraction is a hydrogen bond, and water forms a network of such bonds.

Water molecules gather around any molecule with a full charge (ions) or partial charge (polar molecules):
Sodium chloride: in water NaCl breaks into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; these are surrounded by the opposite polar ends of water molecules (Figure 4.7).
Glucose: water molecules form hydrogen bonds with the polar hydroxyl groups of glucose, so glucose dissolves (Figure 4.8).

So charged or polar (hydrophilic) molecules such as salts, sugars and amino acids dissolve, while non-polar (hydrophobic) lipids do not. In solution ions and molecules react easily, so water provides the medium for metabolism.

book_ref.quote: The ability of water to dissolve a wide variety of substances is due to its two properties

blocks.prompt: 5 Water protects organisms from sudden temperature changes. Explain its high specific heat capacity and high heat of vaporization and how each benefits life. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
High specific heat capacity: specific heat capacity is the number of calories needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance from 15 °C to 16 °C. Water's is high, 4.184 J (twice that of most carbon compounds and nine times that of iron). Most absorbed heat is used to break hydrogen bonds between water molecules; only then do the molecules move freely and the temperature rise.
Benefit: water heats up slowly and holds its temperature longer in a cooler environment, so it is a temperature stabilizer for the internal and external environment of organisms.

High heat of vaporization: the amount of heat needed to change a liquid to gas. For water it is 574 Kcal/kg, i.e. 574 Kcal changes 1 kg of liquid water into vapour. Evaporation of 2 ml out of 1 litre lowers the temperature of the remaining 998 ml by 1 °C.
Benefit: it keeps Earth's temperature moderate and cools plants and animals when they transpire and perspire; every gram evaporated from the body surface removes 574 calories of heat.

book_ref.quote: Water has a high specific heat capacity i.e., 4.184 Joules

blocks.prompt: 6 Explain the following properties of water and their importance for life: (i) cohesion and surface tension (ii) maximum density at 4 °C. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Cohesion: hydrogen bonds make water molecules 'stick together'; this attraction between the same type of molecules is cohesion, and inside water it is high. Plants depend on it to transport water and nutrients from roots to leaves: evaporation from a leaf pulls the water in the xylem vessels, and because of cohesion this pull is relayed through the xylem down to the roots, so water rises against gravity.
Surface tension: hydrogen bonds also give water high surface tension; it behaves as if coated with an invisible film, so the water-strider walks on water without breaking its surface.

(ii) Maximum density at 4 °C: water is densest at 4 °C; below this its density decreases because hydrogen bonds keep the molecules relatively far apart. At 0 °C water freezes and the ice is less dense than liquid water, since hydrogen bonding holds the molecules further apart. In rivers and lakes ice forms on the surface and floats; it acts as an insulator and does not let heat escape from the water beneath, so aquatic organisms are protected.

book_ref.quote: The cohesion of water is important for living world

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain (i) ionization of water and its importance (ii) hydrophobic exclusion and its role in cell membranes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Ionization: when the covalent bonds among the atoms of a water molecule break, water ionizes into hydrogen ions (H⁺) and hydroxyl ions (OH⁻). Normally the reaction is reversible and in equilibrium. At 25 °C, one molecule in each 550 million is ionized, so H⁺ and OH⁻ are each 10⁻⁷ moles/litre in pure water.
Importance: H⁺ and OH⁻ take part in many cell reactions, e.g. hydrolysis of macromolecules. Their relative concentrations set the acidity or alkalinity (pH) of the medium; acids combine with OH⁻ leaving H⁺ (acidic), bases combine with H⁺ leaving OH⁻ (basic). pH affects biochemical reactions, and enzymes work best at a specific pH.

(ii) Hydrophobic exclusion: non-polar or uncharged molecules are insoluble because water does not make hydrogen bonds with them; placed in water, they are moved out by water molecules and make hydrophobic associations with one another. Lipids are insoluble; when excluded from water they make strong associations among themselves, so lipids help to maintain the membranes of cells.

book_ref.quote: At normal conditions, this reaction is reversible and equilibrium is maintained

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe how glucose, galactose, fructose and ribose form ring structures in solution. Explain the alpha and beta forms of D-glucose. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In solution most monosaccharides form rings: an oxygen-bridge develops between two carbon atoms of the same sugar molecule (Figure 4.14).
Glucose: bridge between carbon 1 and 5, giving a six-cornered ring (pyran).
Galactose: bridge between carbon 1 and 5, again a six-cornered pyran ring.
Fructose: bridge between carbon 2 and 5, giving a five-cornered ring (furan).
Ribose: bridge between carbon 1 and 4, giving a five-cornered furan ring.

Alpha and beta D-glucose: the two forms of D-glucose differ only in the direction of the OH group on carbon 1. In α-D-glucose the OH is on the lower side; in β-D-glucose it is on the upper side. Many alpha-D-glucose molecules join to form starch; many beta-D-glucose molecules join to form cellulose.
The Fischer projection shows a sugar in its open chain form, the Haworth projection in its cyclic form.

book_ref.quote: When in solution, most of the monosaccharides form ring structures

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the structure of starch and glycogen as storage polysaccharides. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Starch: the plant storage polysaccharide. It is insoluble and forms starch granules inside plant cells; being insoluble it does not change the water potential of the cells, so they do not take up water by osmosis. Starch is a mixture of:
Amylose: a chain of glucose monomers with 1,4-glycosidic linkages; straight and unbranched, but it coils into a helix.
Amylopectin: a glucose chain with 1,4-glycosidic linkages and branches with 1,6-glycosidic linkages; it has more ends, so it is broken more quickly.
Both amylose and amylopectin are broken down by the enzyme amylase into maltose, at different rates.

Glycogen: the storage polysaccharide made by animals, found mainly in muscles and liver. It is similar to amylopectin: a chain of glucose with 1,4-glycosidic linkages and branches with 1,6-glycosidic linkages. Because it is so highly branched it can be broken down to glucose very quickly.
Starch and glycogen both contain alpha-glucose (OH on carbon 1 sticks down).

book_ref.quote: Starch is not a pure substance, but is a mixture of amylose and amylopectin

blocks.prompt: 10 Cellulose and starch are both chains of glucose. Explain how a small difference in glucose makes cellulose so different from starch in structure, strength and digestion. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Cellulose is found only in plants, as the main component of cell walls. Like starch it is a chain of glucose with 1,4-glycosidic linkages, but of a different isomer of glucose.

book_ref.quote: This apparently tiny difference makes a huge difference in structure and properties

rows: Alpha-glucose: OH on carbon 1 sticks down
Beta-glucose: OH on carbon 1 sticks up; alternate glucose molecules inverted
Alpha 1-4 polymer coils up to form granules
Hundreds of chains linked by hydrogen bonds into microfibrils, which make fibrils
Very strong and rigid; gives strength to plant cells, young plants, paper and cotton
Broken down by amylase into maltose
Beta-glycosidic bond not broken by amylase; needs cellulase; humans cannot digest it (dietary fibre); cows and termites use gut bacteria

blocks.prompt: 11 Besides cellulose, several polysaccharides act as building materials. Describe chitin, pectin and lignin, agar and murein, giving where each is found. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chitin: a modified form of cellulose. Like cellulose it is a polymer of glucose with the same kind of linkage, but each glucose molecule is modified by the addition of a nitrogen-containing group (Figure 4.22). It is found in the exoskeletons of crabs, lobsters and insects and makes the cell wall of fungi. Only a few organisms can digest it.

Pectin and lignin: polysaccharides used as building material, present in the cell walls of plant cells.

Agar: found in the cell walls of red algae. It is used as a thickener in foods and as a medium on which bacteria and fungi are grown in laboratories.

Murein: a sugar-peptide polymer found in the cell walls of prokaryotes.

book_ref.quote: Pectin and Lignin: They are also the polysaccharides used as building material

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe the general structure of an amino acid and explain what gives each amino acid its identity. Classify the amino acids of the human body into essential and non-essential, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Structure: an amino acid is the basic structural unit of proteins. Four groups are attached to the same carbon atom (alpha carbon): an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen (H) and a side group (R) (Figure 4.23).
About 170 types of amino acids occur in living organisms; about 25 may build proteins; most proteins use 20.

Identity: the identity and unique chemical properties of each amino acid are determined by its side group (R), covalently bonded to the alpha carbon. R is a hydrogen atom in glycine and CH₃ in alanine (Figure 4.24).

Classification (of the 20):
Non-essential (eleven, made by our bodies): alanine, arginine, asparagine, aspartic acid, cysteine, glutamic acid, glutamine, glycine, proline, serine and tyrosine.
Essential (nine, cannot be made and must come from food): methionine, valine, tryptophan, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, threonine, phenylalanine and histidine (necessary only for babies).

book_ref.quote: It is an organic molecule, in which four groups

blocks.prompt: 13 Proteins can be classified on the basis of their structure. Compare fibrous and globular proteins in detail, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Proteins can be classified by role (structural and functional) but the recommended classification is based on structure: fibrous and globular proteins (Table 4.4).

book_ref.quote: We can describe the characteristics of both these classes by a comparison in table 4.4

rows: Soluble in salt, acid or base solutions and aqueous alcohol
Silk fibre (webs of silkworm and spider), actin (muscle cells), fibrin (blood clots), keratin (nails, hair, beak, skin), collagen (matrix of connective tissues)
Enzymes (biocatalysts), antibodies (against antigens), some hormones (regulate body activities), haemoglobin (carries oxygen)

blocks.prompt: 14 Proteins carry out virtually all activities of living organisms. Describe eight structural and functional roles of proteins, with an example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Membranes: proteins are an important part of all plasma membranes; channel proteins control movement of materials, e.g. the sodium-potassium pump of neurons controls Na⁺ and K⁺ movement.
2. Structure: fibrous proteins collagen and keratin make almost the whole structure of cartilage and of hair and nails respectively.
3. Enzymes: catalyse metabolism, e.g. proteases break down proteins, polymerases synthesize polymers.
4. Hormones: some are proteins or peptides, e.g. insulin controls blood glucose level, antidiuretic hormone increases water retention by kidneys.
5. Transport: haemoglobin and myoglobin carry O₂ and some CO₂; cytochromes carry electrons in the electron transport chain; albumin maintains the osmotic concentration of blood.
6. Blood clotting: fibrinogen is activated into fibrin on injury; fibrin makes fibres and a clot forms.
7. Contraction: actin and myosin cause muscular contraction; tubulin makes spindle fibres.
8. Defence: antibodies recognize and combine with antigens and make them harmless.
Also, ion-binding proteins store ions (ferritin stores iron, casein stores potassium and calcium), and repressors regulate gene action by preventing synthesis of RNA.

book_ref.quote: Proteins carry out virtually all activities of living organisms

blocks.prompt: 15 Describe the four structural levels of proteins and the bonds that maintain each level. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The levels of protein structure are shown in Figure 4.29.

1. Primary structure: the linear arrangement of amino acids, i.e. the number and sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain, held by peptide bonds. Every protein has a specific primary structure, determined by the order of nucleotides in DNA. Insulin has two chains (alpha 21, beta 30 amino acids); haemoglobin has two alpha (141 each) and two beta (146 each) chains. Even one change (valine in place of glutamic acid at position six of the beta chain) gives sickle cell haemoglobin.

2. Secondary structure: coiling of the chain gives an alpha helix and folding gives a pleated sheet. Both are maintained by hydrogen bonds between amino and carboxyl groups of nearby amino acids.

3. Tertiary structure: the secondary structure folds further into a complicated globular shape, maintained by ionic, hydrogen and disulphide bonds. Hydrophobic (non-polar) amino acids are buried inside and hydrophilic (polar) ones turn out towards water, giving the most stable shape.

4. Quaternary structure: two or more polypeptide chains with tertiary structures are held together by hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds, forming the most complex proteins.

book_ref.quote: The following are different levels at which proteins are built

blocks.prompt: 16 Fatty acids decide the characteristics of acylglycerols. (i) Describe fatty acids and glycerol. (ii) Compare saturated and unsaturated fatty acids and explain why animal fats store more energy than plant oils. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Acylglycerols are esters of fatty acids and an alcohol (glycerol), formed by dehydration synthesis (OH from the acid's carboxyl group, H from the alcohol's -OH). In triacylglycerols three fatty acids are joined to one glycerol.
Glycerol: a 3C alcohol, each carbon bearing a hydroxyl group; its 3 carbons form the backbone to which three fatty acids attach.
Fatty acids: long hydrocarbon chains with an even number of carbons (4-30), ending in a carboxyl (-COOH) group; straight in animals, branched or ringed in plants. Their solubility in organic solvents and melting points increase with the number of carbon atoms.

(ii) Comparison is given in the table. Animal fats contain saturated fatty acids and so more C-H bonds; plant oils contain unsaturated fatty acids with fewer C-H bonds. Since energy is stored in C-H bonds, animal fats contain more energy.

book_ref.quote: Fatty acids: These are responsible for all the characteristics of acylglycerols

rows: No double bond in the hydrocarbon chain
Double bonds (6 maximum) between one or more pairs of carbon atoms
All internal carbons have hydrogen side-groups
Double bonds replace some hydrogens; fewer than the maximum hydrogens
Found in animal fats; more C-H bonds
Found in plant oils; fewer C-H bonds; one double bond = mono-unsaturated, more = poly-unsaturated

blocks.prompt: 17 Describe (i) steroids, with cholesterol and anabolic steroids as examples (ii) prostaglandins and their roles. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Steroids: lipids whose carbon skeleton is bent into four fused rings; all have the same pattern of three 6-cornered rings and one 5-cornered ring.
Cholesterol is a common steroid in animal cell membranes; it maintains membranes, helps in lipid transport and is a precursor of vitamin D, bile acids and steroid hormones (male and female sex hormones, adrenal hormones, corticosteroids).
Anabolic steroids are synthesized steroids resembling testosterone; they build up muscle and bone mass. They were produced in the 1950s to treat general anaemia; some athletes misused them. They are now banned because they cause serious physical and mental problems such as deep depression and liver damage.

(ii) Prostaglandins: lipids that are modified fatty acids, with non-polar tails attached to a five-carbon ring. They occur in many vertebrate tissues as local chemical messengers. Some stimulate smooth muscles to contract and relax; others constrict or expand blood vessels; they are involved in the inflammatory response to infection. Aspirin is a prostaglandin inhibitor, so it reduces inflammation, pain and fever.

book_ref.quote: Steroids are lipids whose carbon skeleton is bent to form four fused rings

blocks.prompt: 18 Describe the roles of lipids in the life of organisms. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Energy: lipids are important sources of energy (ATP) and are the most energy-rich nutrients. One gram of lipids gives 9.5 kilocalories, against 5.6 for protein and 4.1 for carbohydrate. Acylglycerols store energy efficiently because of their many C-H bonds and, being insoluble, are deposited at storage sites; organisms convert glucose into fats or oils for long storage.
2. Membranes: lipids are essential components of all cellular and subcellular membranes (phospholipids such as phosphatidyl choline form the lipid bilayer).
3. Vitamin carriers: they carry fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K for absorption.
4. Fatty acids: lipids are a source of fatty acids needed for various metabolisms.
5. Cushion: they act as a mechanical cushion and support for vital body organs.
6. Insulation: fats beneath the skin insulate the body from extreme temperatures.
7. Steroids: cholesterol maintains membranes, helps lipid transport and is a precursor of vitamin D, bile acids and steroid hormones.
8. Protection: waxes are hydrophobic and act as protective coverings and water barriers on fruits, leaves and animal skin.

book_ref.quote: Lipids are important sources of energy (ATP)

blocks.prompt: 19 Compare DNA and RNA in their sugar, bases, number of strands, location and types. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides; each nucleotide is a nucleoside (nitrogen base + pentose sugar) joined by an ester linkage to phosphoric acid at C-5 of the sugar, and nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkages.

book_ref.quote: There are two main types of nucleic acids i.e., deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA)

rows: Two polynucleotide chains in a double helix
Mainly in chromosomes (nucleus); small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts; cytoplasm in prokaryotes
Three types: mRNA (3-4%), tRNA (10-15%), rRNA (about 80%); work in protein synthesis

blocks.prompt: 20 Nucleotides do more than build nucleic acids. (i) Describe ATP and NAD as nucleotides. (ii) Explain how DNA controls the activities of a cell through its genes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) ATP is a triphosphate nucleotide of adenine: three phosphate groups attached to one ribose sugar. It is the 'energy currency' of the cell; it provides energy by successively detaching two phosphate groups, changing to ADP and then AMP.
NAD (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) is a co-enzyme; it acts as a hydrogen acceptor in oxidation-reduction reactions of the cell.

(ii) DNA is the hereditary material of all organisms (except some viruses) and contains the 'program' that directs all cellular activities. The program is in the form of genes; a gene is a sequence of DNA nucleotides that codes for a polypeptide.
All organisms read and express genes by the same mechanism, the central dogma. First, transcription: information passes from DNA to RNA as an RNA copy of the gene is produced. Second, translation: information in the RNA directs the synthesis of proteins. When a gene is turned ON it is transcribed and translated into specific proteins; in this way DNA controls the properties and activities of the cell.

book_ref.quote: Nucleotides also play other critical roles in the life of cell

blocks.prompt: 21 Compare glycolipids, glycoproteins, lipoproteins and nucleoproteins in their components, the kind of linkage that joins them, and where they occur. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Conjugated molecules are formed by the combination of two or more molecules belonging to different categories.

book_ref.quote: Some important conjugated molecules are as follows

rows: Membranes, blood serum, cellular secretions, cartilage, eyes, skin
Lipids + proteins; hydrophobic interactions (not covalent or ionic bonds)
Basic structural framework of plasma membranes; lipids are transported in blood as very low-density lipoproteins
Histones with DNA form nucleosomes; stabilize chromosomes in eukaryotes and regulate gene expression
